content: In the past 24 months, a country that has maintained effective rabies surveillance and implemented a robust rabies control program for both humans and animals can be considered to have interrupted rabies transmission. The presence of rabies cases caused by non-canine variants does not invalidate the achievement of zero human rabies deaths or the verification of interrupted rabies transmission. To confirm the interruption of rabies transmission, there must be no cases of dog-mediated rabies for at least 24 months, supported by high-quality surveillance that meets international standards. A country can be declared rabies-free if it demonstrates the absence of both dog-mediated and terrestrial rabies cases. This status is based on the absence of indigenous dog-mediated rabies virus (RABV) infections in humans, dogs, cats, or other animals for at least 24 months. Any positive cases must be proven to be spillovers from wildlife through molecular characterization and epidemiological investigation. Imported cases in carnivores do not affect the rabies-free status if the virus source is confirmed as non-indigenous and there is no evidence of secondary dog infections. The ultimate goal for endemic regions is to achieve zero human rabies deaths and interrupt dog-mediated rabies transmission nationally and regionally. Countries are encouraged to self-declare freedom from dog-mediated rabies according to OIE procedures before undergoing verification of interrupted transmission. Globally, rabies elimination efforts have been supported by organizations such as WHO, FAO, OIE, and GARC, which promote a One Health approach. These efforts include setting global standards, mobilizing resources, and providing technical support to national programs. Regional initiatives, such as those in Southeast Asia and the Americas, have focused on mass dog vaccination, improved surveillance, and public awareness campaigns. For example, the Americas have achieved a significant reduction in human and canine rabies cases through coordinated efforts since the 1980s. Innovative tools, such as smartphone-based geospatial technology, have been developed to enhance epidemiological assessments and direct vaccination campaigns to remote areas. Programs like Mission Rabies and World Animal Protection have implemented mass dog vaccination, community education, and humane dog population management in various countries, contributing to the global goal of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. In summary, rabies elimination is achievable through sustained surveillance, vaccination, public awareness, and international collaboration. The lessons learned from successful regional and global initiatives continue to inform strategies for achieving zero human rabies deaths and interrupting rabies transmission worldwide.
